module_title: Mix Processing: Blending, Pasteurization, and Homogenization

lessons.title: Blending and Dissolving Ingredients: Order and Techniques
lessons.body:
Start with clean, food-grade equipment: a stainless steel vat or large plastic bucket, a long-handled whisk or a heavy-duty hand mixer, and a thermometer. Measure all ingredients by weight using a kitchen scale for accuracy. For a 10-litre mix, combine 3.5 kg fresh milk (or reconstituted milk powder: 1 kg powder to 9 litres water), 1.5 kg sugar, 0.5 kg cream (or 0.2 kg butter), 0.2 kg skim milk powder, and 0.05 kg stabilizer/emulsifier blend. If using eggs, use 4 fresh yolks.

Add liquids first: pour milk and cream into the vat. Heat gently to 45Â°Câwarm enough to dissolve solids but not hot enough to cook eggs. Sprinkle milk powder slowly while whisking to avoid lumps. Then add sugar in a steady stream, stirring until fully dissolved. Next, mix stabilizer with a small amount of dry sugar to prevent clumping, then add to the vat. Finally, whisk in egg yolks. For fruit purees or cocoa, add after pasteurization to preserve flavour, but for cocoa powder, mix with sugar before adding.

Use a whisk in a zigzag motion, scraping the bottom and sides. Avoid creating foamâfoam traps air and affects texture. If lumps form, pass the mix through a fine sieve or use a stick blender for 30 seconds. Check temperature: if it drops below 40Â°C, reheat gently. Never let the mix exceed 50Â°C before pasteurization, as this can start cooking the eggs and cause off-flavours.

In rural Africa, where electricity may be intermittent, blend by hand with a strong whisk or use a manual egg beater. For larger batches, a drum with a paddle mixer works. Always use potable water if reconstituting milk. After blending, immediately proceed to pasteurization to prevent bacterial growth. Record the batch details: date, ingredients, and temperatures. This ensures consistency and safety.

lessons.title: High-Temperature Short-Time (HTST) Pasteurization
lessons.body:
HTST pasteurization heats the mix to 80â85Â°C for 15â25 seconds, then rapidly cools it. This kills harmful bacteria like Salmonella and E. coli while preserving flavour. You need a plate heat exchanger or a continuous flow system with a holding tube. For small-scale production, a stainless steel vat with a thermostat-controlled heater and a pump can work, but precise timing is critical.

Start by preheating the mix to 60Â°C in the vat. Then pump it through a heating section where hot water (90â95Â°C) raises the mix to 82Â°C. The mix then flows through a holding tube sized to ensure 20 seconds of residence time. For a flow rate of 1 litre per minute, the tube volume must be 0.33 litres. After holding, the mix passes through a cooling section where chilled water (1â4Â°C) brings it down to 4Â°C within 30 seconds.

Monitor temperature with a calibrated thermometer at the outlet of the holding tube. If temperature drops below 80Â°C, divert the mix back to the startânever let under-pasteurized mix proceed. Use a flow diversion valve for automatic control. In Africa, where power cuts are common, have a backup generator or manual diversion. Clean the heat exchanger daily with a food-grade detergent and sanitize with hot water (85Â°C) or chlorine solution (100 ppm).

HTST is faster and more energy-efficient than batch pasteurization, but requires investment. For a 100-litre batch, HTST takes about 10 minutes versus 30 minutes for batch. However, HTST demands consistent milk quality and careful maintenance. Test pasteurization efficiency monthly using the alkaline phosphatase testâa negative result means proper pasteurization. Always cool immediately to below 4Â°C to prevent recontamination.

lessons.title: Batch Pasteurization and Continuous Systems
lessons.body:
Batch pasteurization (also called low-temperature long-time, LTLT) heats the mix to 63Â°C and holds it for 30 minutes. This is ideal for small-scale producers in Africa because it requires only a vat with a thermostat, a stirrer, and a thermometer. Use a stainless steel or enamel-lined pot. Fill with mix, heat slowly while stirring constantly to prevent scorching. Once the mix reaches 63Â°C, start timing. Maintain 63Â°C for 30 minutesâif temperature drops, extend the holding time. After 30 minutes, cool rapidly by placing the vat in an ice-water bath or using a cooling coil. Stir gently to speed cooling.

Continuous systems, like HTST, use a flow of mix through heating, holding, and cooling sections. They are more efficient for volumes above 500 litres per day. A basic continuous system includes a balance tank, pump, plate heat exchanger, holding tube, and diversion valve. The mix is pumped at a constant rate, heated to 82Â°C for 20 seconds, then cooled to 4Â°C. Continuous systems require less labour and energy per litre, but need reliable electricity and skilled maintenance.

For African conditions, batch pasteurization is more forgiving during power outagesâyou can use firewood or gas to heat. However, it is labour-intensive and risks uneven heating. Always use a calibrated thermometer and stir every 2 minutes. After pasteurization, cool the mix to 4Â°C within 2 hours. Never mix pasteurized with raw mix. Clean all equipment with hot water and detergent, then sanitize with a chlorine solution (100 ppm). Test pasteurization with the alkaline phosphatase test weekly. Record all temperatures and times.

lessons.title: Homogenization: Two-Stage Process and Pressure Settings
lessons.body:
Homogenization breaks fat globules into tiny droplets so they stay mixed and give a smooth texture. Without it, fat rises to the top. You need a homogenizerâa high-pressure pump that forces mix through a narrow valve. For small-scale, a manual or electric homogenizer with a capacity of 100â500 litres per hour works. Two-stage homogenization is standard: first stage at 2000â2500 psi (140â170 bar), second stage at 500 psi (35 bar). The second stage breaks clusters formed in the first stage.

Heat the pasteurized mix to 65â70Â°C before homogenizationâcold mix can damage the machine. Start the homogenizer and let it run with water to check pressure. Then feed the mix. Adjust the first-stage pressure to 2000 psi, then set the second stage to 500 psi. For mix with high fat (above 12%), use 2500 psi first stage. For low-fat mix, 1500 psi is enough. Always maintain constant inlet pressure and temperature. After homogenization, cool the mix immediately to 4Â°C.

In Africa, where equipment may be scarce, some producers use a high-speed blender for 2â3 minutes as a makeshift homogenizer, but this incorporates air and is not as effective. If you cannot homogenize, accept a less creamy product or use more stabilizer. Clean the homogenizer after each use: flush with warm water (50Â°C), then detergent, then sanitize with hot water (85Â°C). Check pressure gauges monthly. Homogenization improves texture, reduces fat separation, and gives a longer shelf life. Record pressures and temperatures for each batch.

lessons.title: Cooling and Aging of Ice Cream Mix
lessons.body:
After pasteurization and homogenization, cool the mix rapidly to 4Â°C or lower. Use a plate cooler, immersion coil, or place the vat in an ice-water bath. Stir gently to speed cooling. The target is to go from 60Â°C to 4Â°C in less than 2 hours. Rapid cooling prevents bacterial growth and helps fat crystallize properly. Once cooled, the mix must be agedâheld at 2â4Â°C for 4 to 24 hours. Aging allows stabilizers to hydrate, fat to crystallize, and proteins to reorient, resulting in smoother ice cream with better overrun.

During aging, keep the mix in a clean, covered stainless steel or plastic container. Do not stir. Maintain temperature between 2Â°C and 4Â°C. Use a refrigerator or a cold room. In rural Africa, a chest freezer with a thermostat or a cool box with ice packs can work if monitored. Check temperature every 4 hours. If temperature rises above 6Â°C, re-cool immediately. Aging for 4 hours is minimum; 12â24 hours is ideal for premium texture.

After aging, the mix is ready for freezing. If you cannot age, add 0.1% more stabilizer to compensate. But aging is crucial for consistency. Record aging time and temperature. Before freezing, check the mix for any off-odours or separation. If separated, re-homogenize. Always use within 48 hours of aging. For large batches, use a jacketed tank with chilled water circulation. Clean and sanitize the aging tank before use. This step is simple but makes a big difference in quality.

lessons.title: Quality Control Tests for Processed Mix
lessons.body:
Quality control ensures your mix is safe and consistent. Test after pasteurization, homogenization, and aging. First, check temperature: mix should be at 4Â°C or below. Use a calibrated thermometer. Second, perform the alkaline phosphatase test to confirm pasteurization. This test uses a kit: add reagent to a mix sample; if it turns yellow, pasteurization failed. If it stays colourless, it passed. Test weekly or when you change suppliers.

Third, check fat content using the Gerber method. For a 10% fat mix, a 10 ml sample should give a reading of 10% on the butyrometer. If fat is low, adjust your recipe. Fourth, measure total solids with a refractometer or by drying a sample. Target 36â40% solids. Fifth, check viscosity: a simple flow testâdip a spoon in the mix and let it drip. It should coat the spoon and drip slowly. If too thick, add water; if too thin, add stabilizer.

Sixth, taste the mix (after pasteurization) for off-flavours. It should be clean, sweet, and creamy. Seventh, check for sediment by filtering 100 ml through a coffee filter; no visible particles. Eighth, test for coliform bacteria using a simple petri film or lab test. Zero colonies is ideal. In Africa, send samples to a local university or health lab monthly. Record all results in a logbook. If any test fails, discard the batch or reprocess. Never sell unsafe ice cream. Good quality control builds customer trust and reduces waste.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Mix Processing for Ice Cream Production in Africa

This practical reference consolidates the six lessons in the Mix Processing module â Blending and Dissolving Ingredients, HTST Pasteurization, Batch and Continuous Pasteurization Systems, Homogenization, Cooling and Aging, and Quality Control Testing â into one field-ready guide. It is written for small and medium ice cream enterprises operating in African markets where ambient temperatures are high, cold-chain reliability varies, and ingredient sourcing can be inconsistent. The goal is simple: help you produce a safe, consistent, saleable mix every single day, at a cost that leaves room for profit.

Mix processing typically accounts for 30â40% of your total production cost and almost all of your food-safety risk. Getting it right protects both your customers and your margins. The figures and tables below give you benchmark values you can post on the production wall.

1. Blending and Dissolving Ingredients â Order and Technique

In African conditions, the biggest blending mistakes are adding powders too fast, using water that is too hot, and failing to pre-blend dry ingredients. The correct sequence:

  1. Heat the liquid phase (milk, water, cream) to 45â55 Â°C â warm enough to dissolve solids, cool enough to avoid scorching and premature protein denaturation.
  2. Pre-blend all dry ingredients (sugar, skim milk powder, stabilizers, emulsifiers) in a dry bucket at a 5:1 sugar-to-stabilizer ratio. This prevents lumping.
  3. Add the dry blend slowly into the vortex of an agitated liquid. Never dump.
  4. Add liquid glucose or invert syrup last, after powders are fully dissolved.
  5. Hold 15â20 minutes with gentle agitation to fully hydrate stabilizers before pasteurization.

Stabilizers (guar, locust bean gum, CMC, carrageenan) hydrate best around 60â70 Â°C, but if you add them above 75 Â°C they can clump irreversibly. If your plant has only one tank, hydrate stabilizers in a small portion of hot liquid first, then combine.

2. Pasteurization â HTST vs Batch

Pasteurization kills pathogens (Salmonella, Listeria, E. coli), inactivates enzymes, and improves mix viscosity. In Africa, batch pasteurization dominates small operations because it requires less capital; HTST suits medium-scale producers with reliable steam and cooling.

Table 1. Pasteurization timeâtemperature combinations for ice cream mix
MethodTemperatureHold TimeTypical ScaleCapital Cost
Batch (vat)69 Â°C30 min50â500 LLow
Batch (vat)80 Â°C25 s50â500 LLow
HTST85 Â°C15 s500â5,000 L/hHigh
HTST (high)90 Â°C30 s500â5,000 L/hHigh
UHT (rare)138 Â°C2 sIndustrialVery high

Source: Codex Alimentarius CXC 57-2004 (Code of Hygienic Practice for Milk and Milk Products); Goff & Hartel, Ice Cream, 7th ed.

Batch systems are forgiving: you can pasteurize in the same vat you blend in, and you can see the mix. But they are slow, energy-hungry, and prone to operator error on hold time. Use a calibrated thermometer and a timer â not your hand.

HTST systems use a plate heat exchanger, a holding tube, and a flow-diversion valve. If the temperature drops below setpoint, the valve sends mix back to the balance tank. This is the single most important safety feature. Never bypass it. HTST also regenerates heat (60â90% recovery), which cuts fuel cost dramatically â a major advantage where electricity or gas is expensive.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Pasteurization and Hot Mix

  • Never open a vat or HTST balance tank during pasteurization. Hot mix at 69â90 Â°C causes severe scalds.
  • Never bypass the flow-diversion valve on an HTST unit. Every bypass is a potential Listeria or Salmonella incident.
  • Verify pasteurization with a phosphatase test weekly. A negative result is your legal proof of safety.
  • Use only food-grade tubing and fittings rated for â¥100 Â°C. Replace cracked gaskets immediately.
  • Wear heat-resistant gloves, apron, and face shield when sampling hot mix.

3. Homogenization â Two-Stage Pressure Settings

Homogenization breaks fat globules from ~3â4 Âµm down to <1 Âµm, preventing cream separation and improving texture. It is done at 65â75 Â°C immediately after pasteurization, using a two-stage valve: a high first stage to break droplets, and a lower second stage to prevent re-aggregation.

Table 2. Recommended two-stage homogenization pressures by mix fat content
Mix TypeFat %1st Stage (bar)2nd Stage (bar)Total (bar)Temp (Â°C)
Low-fat4â61503018065â70
Standard8â102003523570â75
Premium12â142004024070â75
High-fat / gelato16â181804022070â75

Source: Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook (2020); Goff & Hartel, Ice Cream, 7th ed. (2013).

In African plants where power fluctuates, homogenizer pressure can drift. Check gauges every batch. If pressure drops below 150 bar on the first stage, fat globules stay large and your product will churn or separate in the display cabinet â a visible quality failure that customers notice immediately.

4. Cooling and Aging

After homogenization, cool the mix rapidly to 4 Â°C within 2 hours. Slow cooling allows bacteria to multiply and encourages fat crystallization problems. Then age the mix at 2â4 Â°C for 4â24 hours (12â24 hours is ideal). Aging allows:

  • Fat to crystallize (improves overrun and texture)
  • Stabilizers to fully hydrate (improves viscosity and meltdown)
  • Proteins to re-structure after homogenization

In hot African climates, aging tanks must be jacketed or kept in a cold room. A mix aged at 8 Â°C overnight will not behave the same as one aged at 3 Â°C. Temperature discipline here directly affects your yield and your customer's perception of quality.

5. Quality Control Tests for Processed Mix

Run these tests on every batch before freezing:

  • Fat content â Gerber or Babcock method. Target Â±0.2% of specification.
  • Total solids â Refractometer or oven-dry method. Target 36â40%.
  • pH â 6.3â6.6 for fresh mix. Lower values indicate bacterial activity.
  • Viscosity â Brookfield viscometer at 4 Â°C. Aged mix should be noticeably thicker than fresh.
  • Phosphatase â Must be negative. This is your legal pasteurization proof.
  • Homogenization index â NIZO or microscopic check for fat globule size.
  • Total plate count â <10,000 CFU/mL after pasteurization.
  • Coliforms â Absent in 1 mL. Any positive result means re-clean and re-pasteurize.

In markets where regulators inspect, keep written records for at least 6 months. Buyers and supermarkets increasingly demand this as a condition of supply.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. â Pre-blend dry ingredients before adding to liquid at 45â55 Â°C.
  2. â Pasteurize at 85 Â°C / 15 s (HTST) or 69 Â°C / 30 min (batch); never bypass diversion valve.
  3. â Homogenize at 200/35 bar at 70â75 Â°C immediately after pasteurization.
  4. â Cool to 4 Â°C within 2 hours; age at 2â4 Â°C for 4â24 hours.
  5. â Run phosphatase test every batch â must be negative.
  6. â Check fat, total solids, pH, and viscosity against specifications.
  7. â Record all parameters in a batch log; keep for 6 months minimum.
  8. â Clean and sanitize all contact surfaces before the next batch begins.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO â Milk and Dairy Products in Human Nutrition
  • Codex Alimentarius â Code of Hygienic Practice for Milk and Milk Products (CXC 57-2004)
  • US FDA â Grade "A" Pasteurized Milk Ordinance (PMO) reference
  • Dairy Science & Food Technology â open educational resource
  • Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook (free online edition)

Bottom line for African producers: mix processing is where safety, texture, and margin are decided. Master the temperature and pressure setpoints, document every batch, and your ice cream will be consistent enough to win shelf space in supermarkets and loyal customers in your own outlet.

quiz.q: What is the recommended order for blending ice cream mix ingredients?
options: A) Dry ingredients first, then liquids
B) Liquids first, then dry ingredients
quiz.explanation: Liquids are added first to dissolve dry ingredients evenly and prevent lumps.

quiz.q: At what temperature should you heat milk and cream before adding dry ingredients?
quiz.explanation: 45Â°C is warm enough to dissolve solids without cooking eggs or causing off-flavours.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid creating foam when blending?
options: A) Foam makes the mix too sweet
B) Foam traps air and affects texture
quiz.explanation: Foam incorporates air, which can lead to inconsistent texture and overrun.

quiz.q: What is the holding time and temperature for HTST pasteurization?
quiz.explanation: HTST uses 80â85Â°C for 15â25 seconds to kill pathogens while preserving quality.

quiz.q: What should you do if the mix temperature drops below 80Â°C during HTST?
options: C) Divert the mix back to the start
quiz.explanation: Under-pasteurized mix must be reprocessed to ensure safety.

quiz.q: Which test confirms proper pasteurization?
quiz.explanation: Alkaline phosphatase is an enzyme inactivated by proper pasteurization.

quiz.q: What is the typical holding time and temperature for batch pasteurization?
quiz.explanation: Batch pasteurization uses 63Â°C for 30 minutes to achieve pasteurization.

quiz.q: Why is batch pasteurization suitable for small-scale African producers?
options: A) It requires less equipment and can use firewood
B) It is faster than HTST
quiz.explanation: Batch pasteurization needs only a vat and heat source, making it accessible during power outages.

quiz.q: What is the first stage pressure for two-stage homogenization?
quiz.explanation: First stage pressure is typically 2000â2500 psi to break fat globules.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the second stage in homogenization?
options: A) To further reduce fat globule size
B) To break clusters formed in the first stage
quiz.explanation: The second stage at lower pressure breaks clusters formed during the first stage.

quiz.q: What temperature should the mix be before homogenization?
quiz.explanation: Warm mix at 65â70Â°C homogenizes more effectively and prevents machine damage.

quiz.q: How long should ice cream mix be aged?
quiz.explanation: Aging for 4â24 hours allows stabilizers to hydrate and fat to crystallize.

quiz.q: What is the ideal aging temperature for ice cream mix?
quiz.explanation: Aging at 2â4Â°C ensures proper crystallization and prevents bacterial growth.

quiz.q: What happens if you skip aging?
options: A) The ice cream will be too hard
B) The texture will be less smooth
C) The mix will not freeze
D) The flavour will be too strong
quiz.explanation: Without aging, stabilizers don't fully hydrate, leading to icy texture.

quiz.q: Which of these is a quality control test for processed mix?
quiz.explanation: All these tests check different aspects of mix quality and safety.

quiz.q: What does the Gerber test measure?
quiz.explanation: The Gerber test determines fat percentage in the mix.

quiz.q: What is the target total solids for ice cream mix?
quiz.explanation: 36â40% total solids gives good body and texture in ice cream.

quiz.q: How can you check viscosity of the mix simply?
options: B) Dip a spoon and observe drip
quiz.explanation: A spoon drip test gives a quick indication of thickness.

quiz.q: What should you do if the alkaline phosphatase test turns yellow?
options: B) Discard or reprocess the mix
quiz.explanation: Yellow indicates incomplete pasteurization, making the mix unsafe.

quiz.q: Why is rapid cooling important after pasteurization?
quiz.explanation: Rapid cooling to 4Â°C prevents surviving bacteria from multiplying.

quiz.q: What is the maximum time allowed for cooling mix from 60Â°C to 4Â°C?
quiz.explanation: Cooling within 2 hours minimizes bacterial growth.

quiz.q: Which equipment is used for continuous pasteurization?
quiz.explanation: Plate heat exchangers are core to continuous HTST systems.

quiz.q: What is the flow rate for a holding tube with 0.33 litres volume and 20 seconds holding time?
quiz.explanation: 0.33 litres in 20 seconds equals 1 litre per minute.

quiz.q: What is a common makeshift homogenizer in small-scale production?
quiz.explanation: A high-speed blender can partially homogenize, though it incorporates air.

quiz.q: How often should you test pasteurization efficiency with alkaline phosphatase?
quiz.explanation: Weekly testing ensures ongoing pasteurization effectiveness.

quiz.q: What should you do if the mix separates after aging?
quiz.explanation: Re-homogenization can re-emulsify separated fat.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature for storing pasteurized mix before freezing?
quiz.explanation: 2â4Â°C keeps mix safe and ready for freezing.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a quality control test for mix?
quiz.explanation: Packaging colour is not a quality test for the mix itself.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding stabilizer during blending?
options: B) To improve texture and prevent ice crystals
quiz.explanation: Stabilizers bind water and inhibit ice crystal growth.

quiz.q: What is the recommended maximum temperature for mix before pasteurization?
quiz.explanation: Above 50Â°C, eggs may cook and cause off-flavours.
